pages.text: Zumah woke up with a runny nose. She sneezed, “Achoo!” right into the air. Her little brother giggled. “Your sneeze went all over me!” he said. Auntie Dzobo came in. “Let us talk about that.”
sentences: Zumah woke up with a runny nose.
She sneezed, “Achoo!” right into the air.
Her little brother giggled.
“Your sneeze went all over me!” he said.
Auntie Dzobo came in.
“Let us talk about that.”
pages.alt: In a sunny Ghanaian morning room, young Zumah in a lilac shirt sneezes into the air while her little brother leans back giggling and Auntie Dzobo steps in kindly.

pages.text: “When we cough or sneeze, tiny drops fly out of our nose and mouth,” said Auntie Dzobo. “They can carry germs. If someone breathes them in, they can catch a cold too.” Zumah’s eyes grew wide.
sentences: “When we cough or sneeze, tiny drops fly out of our nose and mouth,” said Auntie Dzobo.
“They can carry germs.
If someone breathes them in, they can catch a cold too.” Zumah’s eyes grew wide.
pages.alt: Sitting beside wide-eyed Zumah, Auntie Dzobo holds up a simple wordless picture card showing tiny blue droplets spraying through the air.

pages.text: “Cough or sneeze into your elbow or into a clean cloth,” said Auntie Dzobo. “Then throw the cloth away or wash it. Wash your hands with soap after you cough, sneeze or blow your nose.” Zumah practised.
sentences: “Cough or sneeze into your elbow or into a clean cloth,” said Auntie Dzobo.
“Then throw the cloth away or wash it.
Wash your hands with soap after you cough, sneeze or blow your nose.” Zumah practised.
pages.alt: Zumah practises tucking her nose and mouth neatly into her bent elbow while Auntie Dzobo smiles approvingly beside a basin of water and soap.

pages.text: “If you feel sick, tell a grown-up and stay at home and rest,” said Auntie Dzobo. “Drink water. If you still feel bad, or if you have trouble breathing, go to the clinic.” Zumah rested for two days.
sentences: “If you feel sick, tell a grown-up and stay at home and rest,” said Auntie Dzobo.
“Drink water.
If you still feel bad, or if you have trouble breathing, go to the clinic.” Zumah rested for two days.
pages.alt: Resting comfortably under a light colourful cloth on a sofa at home, Zumah holds a clean cup of water while Auntie Dzobo sits beside her.

pages.text: Back at school, Zumah showed her class what she had learned. “Cover your cough, wash your hands and stay home if you are sick,” she said. The class drew bright pictures of how to be a Cough Catcher, and everyone practised.
sentences: Back at school, Zumah showed her class what she had learned.
“Cover your cough, wash your hands and stay home if you are sick,” she said.
The class drew bright pictures of how to be a Cough Catcher, and everyone practised.
pages.alt: In her yellow-and-brown school uniform, healthy Zumah shows her smiling classmates how to cough into a bent elbow beside a wordless picture chart of elbow-coughing and soapy hands.

pages.text: Soon, the class had fewer colds. “We keep each other well,” said Zumah. “A cough catcher cares about others.” She smiled, and washed her hands before lunch.
sentences: Soon, the class had fewer colds.

pages.alt: Outside the classroom before lunch, Zumah and her cheerful classmates wash their hands with white soap bubbles at a clean Veronica bucket.
